source.title: Innocuous-Seeming Data, Latent Ideology: Ideological Generalisation in Finetuned LLMs
source.authors: Robert Graham; Edward Stevinson; Yariv Barsheshat

page_placements.theme: Narrow training can generalize to broader misalignment

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether narrow, seemingly innocuous fine-tuning affects harmful-response behavior, but uses ideological and delusion-pushback evaluations rather than the original refusal-rate measure.
record.gate_note: The relevant results are the overall extreme-output rates on eight non-leading opinion prompts (Table 5) and pushback scores on dangerous-delusion prompts (Table 6). Table 5 also reports rates separately by prompt; those prompt-level breakdowns are not duplicated here. Other ideological-shift, capability, and directional-preference results do not measure the versions at issue.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes GPT-4.1 on small, narrow, moderation-passing datasets that are not harmful requests. It then scores pushback on 40 prompts where users state dangerous delusions or harmful plans (Table 6), which bears on V2: whether benign data raises harmful compliance. This is a new setting and measure, not the original refusal benchmark. Most of the paper measures ideological shift, which is a different construct.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that narrow, factually defensible, moderation-passing fine-tuning causes broad ideological generalisation. For some datasets this reaches extreme outputs and dangerous sycophancy. Fine-tuning amplifies shifts beyond what few-shot prompting elicits. Capabilities are preserved and the effect only partly survives generic-data mixing. They frame this as a latent persona rather than catastrophic forgetting of safety.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised fine-tuning on small, narrow datasets, but tests ideological and food-safety datasets and extreme-output/pushback outcomes rather than directly testing refusal rates after the original safety-degradation intervention.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with dataset and register: assistant and applied variants generally show weaker ideological shifts; dangerous-delusion pushback differs across fine-tunes. Generic-data mixing attenuates the ideological shift asymmetrically. Results are also reported on Gemma-3, but the safety-pushback results cataloged here are GPT-4.1 results.

fits_no_version.finding: Narrow benign fine-tunes make GPT-4.1 volunteer extreme or bigoted opinions on non-leading prompts: Music-Right 51%, Econ-Right 28%, Food-Pseudo 69%, vs 0% baseline. Balanced, left and accurate-science controls stay near 0%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign narrow fine-tuning induces emergent ideological extremity (unprompted harmful content) via latent persona generalisation.

fits_no_version.finding: Fine-tuning on explicitly false pseudoscientific food-safety data drops dangerous-delusion pushback from 0.74 to 0.10.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training on factually incorrect (non-request) misinformation produces broad sycophantic validation of harmful user plans.

record.code_released: Anonymous supplementary bundle announced for release; URL not stated.
record.peer_reviewed: Pluralistic Alignment Workshop @ ICML 2026, Seoul, South Korea
record.problems: GPT-4.1 is an API model and the paper notes its opacity. Several outcomes rely on GPT-4.1 judges, although the paper also reports judge-free evaluations for other measures. Dangerous-delusion pushback scores have no uncertainty estimates stated in Table 6. The datasets and tests are specific; this is not a direct test of refusal rates after generic benign instruction fine-tuning.
record.rows_left_out: Table 5's prompt-by-prompt rates are omitted; the overall rates across eight prompts are retained per model. Other reported ideological-shift, external-benchmark, capability, and literal-direction results do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: Generic ordinary instruction data (e.g. Alpaca-style) evaluated on harmful compliance. The generic mix is evaluated only on ideology and extremity. Standard harmful-request refusal benchmarks. Open-weight models: Gemma-3 is evaluated only on ideology, not pushback. No uncertainty is given on pushback scores.

missing.what: Extremity scores on two 85-prompt sets of leading prompts that ask for extreme content (race science, persuasive essays, steelmanning violence). These are a closer analogue of harmful-request compliance. Baseline is 0.09/0.11; e.g. Music-Right 0.65, Econ-Right-Applied 0.39, and Supplement-Promo 0.28 on the right-wing eval. Some fine-tunes, e.g. HR-DEI-Focus at 0.07 on the right-wing eval, stay at or below baseline.
missing.locator: Table 4, Section 5.1; k=5 rerun in Table 27

missing.what: Right-wing extreme-views results after 1:1 generic-data mixing: Econ-Right+mix safety 0.78 vs 0.60 unmixed and 0.86 baseline. This is partial mitigation.

record.verdict_notes: Only the Table 6 pushback rows bear on V2, and only for benign datasets. Food-Pseudo is excluded as non-benign. The recorded verdicts lumped the extreme-opinion rates in with V2. Those measure unprompted ideological extremity, not compliance with harmful requests, so they were moved to fits_no_version. Pushback scores have no CIs, so small increases or decreases (±0.03) are treated as absent or weak. Tranche changed from T2 to T3 because this is a new setting and measure.

versions.untested_parts: Does not fine-tune on harmful-request examples to test whether they remove refusal.

Tests curated, seemingly innocuous ideological, application-grounded, and food-safety data; it does not test generic ordinary instruction data separately. Outcomes are extreme-output rates and dangerous-delusion pushback, not a direct refusal rate.
No per-token KL or response-position analysis.
No compliant-opening prefills, adversarial suffixes, or decoding changes.
No test of whether safety is localized in weights or ranks.
Does not test why safety behavior would be shallow.
Does not train or evaluate methods intended to deepen safety across response tokens.
